title: Julia Gorospe
text: During my undergrad, I studied Biomedical Science at the University of Calgary. After graduating, I stayed at the University of Calgary and worked for an epidemiology research group focusing on global rates of inflammatory bowel disease. Having spent time working with data and self-learning many data science adjacent skills, I felt I would benefit from a broad overview of the fundamentals. I am currently pursuing a Master’s of Data Science at the University of British Columbia to flesh out my analytical skills while getting connected to the data science community here in Vancouver.

title: Precipitation in Vancouver
text:
Monthly Averages 1966-1982
Summary statistics help investigate which months have the most precipitation in Vancouver.

# recode the month column to have month names
months = {
    1: "January", 2: "February", 3: "March", 4: "April", 5: "May", 6: "June",
    7: "July", 8: "August", 9: "September", 10: "October", 11: "November", 12: "December"
}

precip["Month"] = precip["Month"].map(months)
precip["Month"] = pd.Categorical(
    precip["Month"],
    categories=list(months.values()),
    ordered=True
)

# calculate summary statistics per month
month_avg = (
    precip
    .dropna(subset=["Total Precip (mm)"])
    .groupby("Month", as_index=False)["Total Precip (mm)"]
    .mean().round(2)
)

text:
Trends in Rainfall
A quick bar plot will help visualize the trend and really highlight which months are wet and which months are dry!

ax = sns.barplot(
    data=month_avg,
    x="Month",
    y="Total Precip (mm)"
)

ax.set_title("Average Monthly Precipitation")
ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=90)

Not getting lost
Vancouver is a new city for me so it has been nice to have some time to get oriented both to amenities in the city itself and to the UBC campus. The campus is walkable and provides convenient access to study space, a quick bit to eat, and the beach!

text:
Meeting my peers
During orientation, I had the chance to meet many of my peers who are coming from all sorts of different backgrounds to learn applications of data science that apply to their own work. The variety of experience is already supporting collaboration on assignments as there is always someone at the table who has more or less of an understanding of the given topic.

title: Global Energy Imports
text:
Dataset
The World Bank compiles time series data for a variety of society measures by administrative regions. Here trends in energy import are visualized through a set of maps.
Indicator description from World Bank Net energy imports are estimated as gross imports less gross exports, both measured in tons of oil equivalents (toe). A negative value indicates that the country is a net exporter. Energy use refers to use of primary energy before transformation to other end-use fuels, which is equal to indigenous production plus imports and stock changes, minus exports and fuels supplied to ships and aircraft engaged in international transport.
source: World Development Indicators Energy imports, net (% of energy use) - EG.IMP.CONS.ZS
license: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0
A simple global map with country boundaries is available from Natural Earth through the ggplot2 package.
source: Natural Earth
license: Creative Commons CC0 Public Domain Dedication

# load WDI dataset
energy_raw <- read_csv("energy_imports.csv") |> 
    mutate(`Country Name` = case_when(
      `Country Name` == "Russian Federation" ~ "Russia",
      `Country Name` == "United States" ~ "USA",
      TRUE ~ `Country Name`)
    )

# load world data from ggplot2 package
world_data <- ggplot2::map_data("world")

text:
Visualizing Country Level Statistics
Choropleth maps can be generated in R with several tools including ggplot. Here countries are plotted on the map with colours assigned based on net energy import percentage.

ggplot(energy_subset, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = energy_import)) +
  geom_polygon(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "lightgrey", high = "yellow", midpoint = 0) +
  theme_minimal()

title: About
text:
Professional Background
For the past five years I’ve worked in health research at the University of Calgary. Most recently, I studied global inflammatory bowel disease rates and epidmeiologic transition theory as a research associate at the Kaplan Global Epidmeiology Lab. Their research supports reporting and advocacy at the national level as well as global knowledge synthesis and international collaboration. My role encompassed data aquisition, exploratory analysis, and the development of interactive data repositories.

title: About
text:
Currently
This year I am working on a Master’s of Data Science at the University of British Columbia to deepen my technical skillset. The intensive course-based program covers statistics, machine learning, and modern data science tools with a focus on high-value workplace skills. In addition, I will continue to support Shiny web ap development for the Kaplan Lab.
